anchored.1: I, Apollo, proclaim to all gods and all mortal men: I shall give a golden basin to whoever can bring back my cattle from far away.
anchored.10: It is quite unpleasant to me that they are gone, all of them: cows, calves, heifers. They are all gone, and I look in vain for their tracks, while they wander far from their own mangers. I never thought that any of the gods or of men, whose lives are like a single day, would dare do such a thing. Since I found out about this, shocked as I was, I have been seeking them, and I have proclaimed the deed
anchored.20: so that no god or mortal men could be unaware of it. I am beside myself. I have gone to visit the whole nation of the Locrians, those who inhabit Opus, those in Ozolis, those in Knemis by the Cephisus. I have gone to Aetolia and to Acarnanian Argos. From there I came to the grove of Zeus at Dodona, shaded by leaves of prophecy. I then hastened to the fruitful plains of Thessaly
anchored.30: and the wealthy cities of Boeotia. And then I came to Attica, to holy Athens, but I see my cows nowhere. Then I came to Dorian Argos and the nearby hill. From there I came, in one leap, to the Stymphalian Lake and Mount Cyllene, hard to climb. I speak to the forest: if any shepherd or any rustic or any charcoal-burner is here,
anchored.40: or any saytr from the mountains, child of the river-nymphs, I announce these things to one and all. Whoever can capture the one who stole the cattle of Apollo Paean, his is the reward that stands here.
anchored.45: As soon as I heard you shouting your proclamation, I came as fast as an old man can, because I want to help you out, Phoebus Apollo,
anchored.50: and perhaps I can hunt up your cattle. Then a messenger will announce my golden reward. I will tell my children to look carefully, if you really do mean to do what you’ve promised.
anchored.55: I will indeed; only confirm your promise.
anchored.56: I will bring you back your cattle; but you confirm the reward.
anchored.57: Whoever finds them will have it; it is ready at hand.
anchored.63: I say that you, and all the race of your children, will be free.
anchored.64: Come, come here, see if you can find the footprints of the lost cattle. Apapapay! Oh, oh, listen, I tell you! Get the thief! underground
anchored.70: finish the job my old father. How can we find out the secret thefts in the night? if I did meet free life for my father. So may the dear god bring an end to my labors, as he has shown us the extraordinary excellence of his gold.
anchored.79: Oh gods, Fortune and the god who leads in the straight way, grant me success as I race out to seek out the prey, the spoil, and the booty: the cattle stolen from Phoebus. If there is anyone who has seen them, or heard about them, he would become my friend by telling me, and he would help me to help lord Phoebus. But if someone does not tell what he knows, his reward will be the god’s disapproval.
anchored.91: Does anyone say, or does anyone know, where the cattle are? It seems that I must begin the search. Come, all of you, track them by their scent, if there is any trace left anywhere. Bent over, crouching to the ground, be guided by the scent. Carry out your search this way and bring it to a worthy fulfilment.
anchored.100: Oh god, oh god, oh god, oh god: aha! We seem to have it. Stand still, don’t move.
anchored.102: There they are: the marks of the cattle.
anchored.103: Quiet! Some god is taking them to a new home.
anchored.104: What should we do, my friend? Do we have to get them out?
anchored.105: Why? Do you think they’re in here?
anchored.105b: Definitely. All the signs say so clearly.
anchored.107: Look! Here’s the same hoof mark again.
anchored.110: They measure out to exactly the same size.
anchored.111: Make way, and if you hear any sound from the cattle.
anchored.114: I don’t yet hear their voices clearly. But these tracks and footprints are obviously those of the cattle.
anchored.117: Hey! As Zeus is my witness, the tracks turn around and go backward. Look at them.
anchored.120: Why is that? Why would their line wheel around? The front is turned to the back, and they’re all tangled up together. The cowherd must have been awfully confused.
anchored.124: What kind of a way to hunt is that, bent over and leaning down to the ground? Where are you going? I don’t understand. You’re lying there like a hedgehog fallen on the ground, or an ape sticking his head forward and having a temper tantrum. What’s this? Where on earth did you learn this, and how?
anchored.130: Tell me, because I certainly don’t understand what you’re doing.
anchored.132: What are you ooh-ooh-ing for? What are you afraid of? What do you see? What frightful thing are you looking at? Why are you carrying on like bacchantes? Is there a hawk nearby? Do you want to know what it was? Why are you so quiet, when you were just now babbling away?
anchored.137: What is it over there that you’re trying to get away from?
anchored.139: I’ll listen. But I don’t hear any sound.
anchored.141: No one is helping me with this hunt.
anchored.142: Listen just a moment, will you? When we went over there we were assaulted by a noise like no one ever heard before.
anchored.145: Why are you running away, afraid of a noise? You wretched beasts, with your filthy bodies all smeared with wax, seeing terrors in every shadow, scared of everything! You’re gutless, and careless,
anchored.150: and servile. You’re nothing but body and tongue and voice. You trust to words and flee from actions. Worst of animals, how did you ever come to have a father like me? There are lots of monuments to my courage, when I was young, songs sung at every household’s wedding feast. I was never put to flight, never afraid, and I didn’t quiver at noises made by animals up on the mountains. Instead, I accomplished great things with my spear. That brilliant spear is now besmirched by you,
anchored.160: because some new sound from the shepherds has frightened you, like the babies you are, and you’ve given up on the golden wealth that Phoebus said he was offering to you, to say nothing of freedom, which he also offered to you and to me. You’ve put all that away and gone to sleep. Unless you get back to work tracking those cows and their cowherd, wherever they are, you’ll be making noises of your own for your cowardice.
anchored.170: so you’ll know whether I’m really a coward. If you’re here, you’ll know first hand, not through rumors.
anchored.172: I will approach this sound with you, and I will call out and whistle as I’d call a dog. You, line up three by three, and I will go beside you and get you straightened out again.
anchored.176: Ooh, ooh, ooh, ssh, ssh, aah, aah! Say what you’re working on. Why did you shout and scream? It’s pointless. And why were you suspicious of me? Who’s holding back in our first task?
anchored.180: You are. He came, he came. You are mine; lead the way. This way, ho! Who is the ? The dragon, the wrinkled one Goddess of fair winds, you were beside me, drunk Whatever bring set on top of it the way which warlike
anchored.190: Follow me, this way! To the cows, to the task so he doesn’t drop the saffron You see something beautiful and the good lawful Follow me Oppopopoy! Hey, filthy polluted one! As soon as you get away from here, you’ll be set free and
anchored.200: But don’t get lost Come on, straight ahead, this way. Now we’ve got the crook.
anchored.203: Father, why are you quiet? Isn’t what we’re saying true? Aren’t you listening? Or are you deafened by the noise?
anchored.206: No way. But you go ahead: you keep looking and track down the cows, any way you want to, and take the gold unless the biggest time.
anchored.210: No, I won’t leave you, nor sneak away from the work, before we know for sure what’s going on in there.
anchored.213: Hey! You in there! voice reward you will be happy at home. He’s not coming out. But I’ll force you out, making the ground rumble with my swift leaps and kicks,
anchored.220: so you’ll listen, even if you’re altogether deaf.
anchored.221: Satyrs, why have you rushed up here making all this noise, on this mountain covered with green woods full of animals? Have you got yourselves a new job? You used to bring joy to your master, who would put on a fawn skin and carry a thyrsus in his hands. You would dance around the god shouting Evoe, along with the nymphs, who are his family, and a crowd of children. But now I don’t know what you’re doing. Where is this whirlwind
anchored.230: of new craziness taking you? I heard something odd: first, nearby, orders like you’d give to hunting dogs when they get near a wild animal’s den in a thicket; then, at the same time, stretched out from the mouth to the thief . Then announcement . After that they went away, feet stomping, and a confused sound came from nearby. It would be different if
anchored.240: So I heard the sounds of wrong notes you sick you did to a nymph that had nothing to do with it?
anchored.243: Deep-girdled nymph, don’t be angry. No one’s starting a war with you, nor has any unfriendly or trifling word touched my tongue. Please don’t threaten me, but graciously tell me what I need: who is it
anchored.250: who seems to speak in a wonderful, inspired voice from below the earth?
anchored.251: That’s better: you sound gentler now. You would learn more by hunting rather than from a coward’s great deeds or a nymph’s ordeal. I won’t put up with your loud, quarrelsome words. But calm down and tell me what it is you need.
anchored.258: Mighty Cyllene, lady of this land, I’ll tell you in a moment why I’ve come.
anchored.260: But first tell us about that scraping noise and who’s making it.
anchored.262: First of all, understand this: if you say one word of what I’m about to tell you, you’ll be in trouble. This business is a secret even among the gods, so that no news of it may come to Hera. You see, Zeus came secretly to Atlas’s house
anchored.270: to the deep-girdled goddess and in a cave begot a single son. I am bringing him up myself, for his mother’s strength is shaken by sickness as if by a storm. So I stay by his crib and take care of his food and drink and rest, all day and all night. He grows, day by day, in a very unusual way, and I’m astounded and afraid. It’s not even six days since he was born,
anchored.280: and he already stands as tall as a young man. His growth spurt hasn’t wasted any time coming. That’s the kind of child that’s in my treasure-house. His father has ensured he would be difficult to find. He has a hidden machine that makes the sound you’re asking about, that so surprised you. It’s a box full of pleasure that he made in just one day from a dead animal he found, and he’s down there shaking it.
anchored.290: unspeakable child of a cow amazed prey speaking voice to make such sounds from a dead animal.
anchored.298: Don’t be so skeptical: for a goddess is speaking trusty words to you.
anchored.300: How should I believe that a dead animal’s voice can roar like that?
anchored.301: Believe it: it speaks now it’s dead, though it had no voice when it was alive.
anchored.302: What did it look like? Long, curved, short?
anchored.303: Short, like a pitcher, and covered with a colorful hide.
anchored.304: Was it like a cat, or rather a leopard?
anchored.305: In between, really: it’s round with short legs.
anchored.306: Closer to a ferret, then, or a crab?
anchored.307: No, that’s not it; try something else.
anchored.308: Is it like one of the horned beetles that live on Aetna?
anchored.309: Now you’re getting closer to the beast
anchored.310: And which part makes the sound, the inside or the outside?
anchored.312: What name do you call it? Tell me, if you know any more.
anchored.313: The boy calls the animal a tortoise and the instrument a lyre.
anchored.314b: and this is his only consolation or cure for sorrow. He enjoys idly singing along; he coaxes Aeolian tunes from the lyre. Thus the boy made himself a voice from a dead animal.
